synopsis: Flight crew fatigue on night approach
narrative: During a night approach into a busy Class B airport at the end of a long duty day, the First Officer and I were both fatigued. I was flying and became fixated on the localizer, briefly descending below the glideslope. The FO called out "below glidepath" and I corrected. We had been awake nearly 16 hours. Fatigue clearly degraded my scan and situational awareness on the approach. Better duty-time management and a stronger sterile-cockpit discipline would have helped.

synopsis: Runway incursion after ambiguous taxi instruction
narrative: Ground control issued a taxi instruction to cross runway 27R that we found ambiguous in heavy traffic. We began to cross while another aircraft was on short final. Tower issued an immediate go-around to the landing traffic. In hindsight the taxi clearance should have been read back more carefully and we should have confirmed the hold-short instruction. Signage at the intersection was faded and hard to read at night, contributing to the runway incursion.

We were high and fast on final due to a late runway change and a tailwind. The approach was unstable through 500 feet but we elected to continue rather than go around. We landed long and used heavy braking, stopping with limited margin. Company policy calls for a go-around when unstable below 500 feet AGL. We normalized the deviation because the weather was good and we felt pressure to stay on schedule.

synopsis: Altitude deviation from distraction in cruise
narrative: In cruise the flight attendant called about a passenger medical issue. Both pilots became involved in coordinating with dispatch and medical services. During the distraction we missed a crossing restriction and descended 700 feet below our assigned altitude before ATC queried us. We climbed back immediately. The workload from the medical event pulled our attention off primary flight duties; one pilot should have remained heads-down on aircraft control.

synopsis: Engine oil pressure fluctuation and precautionary diversion
narrative: About one hour into the flight we observed the number 2 engine oil pressure fluctuating near the low end of the normal band. The oil temperature remained normal. Following the QRH we reduced thrust on the affected engine and elected a precautionary diversion to a suitable airport. The landing was uneventful. Maintenance later found a faulty oil pressure transducer. Erring toward a precautionary diversion was the right call given the ambiguous indication.

Just after rotation we experienced multiple bird strikes, with impacts on the radome and the left engine. We heard a compressor surge from the left engine and saw a brief EGT spike, then parameters stabilized. We declared an emergency, ran the appropriate checklists, and returned for an overweight landing. Post-flight inspection found ingested bird remains and minor fan blade damage. The airport had reported bird activity earlier that morning.

synopsis: Confusion over automation mode on descent
narrative: During descent we were cleared to a lower altitude but the aircraft did not begin descending. We had left the automation in a mode that held altitude, and neither pilot noticed the mode annunciation. ATC repeated the clearance and we then descended. This automation-mode confusion is a recurring human-factors issue; clearer verbalization of mode changes and cross-checking the FMA would have caught it sooner.

synopsis: Icing encounter and airspeed indication anomaly
narrative: In cruise near the top of a cloud layer we encountered moderate icing that the forecast had not indicated. We noticed an airspeed disagreement between the captain and first officer displays. We turned on all anti-ice systems, exited the icing conditions with a climb, and the indications returned to agreement. We suspect a partially blocked pitot probe. Unexpected icing and the resulting unreliable airspeed made this a high-workload event.
